With a federal reorientation of energy, environmental justice, and disaster funding, the importance of the F3 project increased because the resulting planning approaches can be market-based and agnostic of the renewable energy policy environment and represents flexible approaches that can be applied at multiple scales to synergistically increase community resilience. The primary objectives of the F3 project were accomplished through concurrent top- down (asset-based) and bottom-up (community-based) research. Project results included the establishment of resilient power siting criteria rubric, financial modeling for a portfolio of potential developments, community-based participatory research into previous grid-outages and future resilience needs, creation of minimum resilience standards for the Duluth community, and a planning toolkit that was vetted by other Midwest communities to deepen governmental and community-based renewable and resilience approaches. 3 Table of Contents Cover Page Background The term “low-attention disasters” has been coined to convey the experience of Midwestern communities that often face multiple smaller disaster events that often do not qualify for federal or state support. These events can hit small cities and sparsely populated rural areas that lack the density of services and capacity for planning that is available in larger urban areas and hurricane prone geographies. The cumulative impact of these low-attention disasters reaches billions of dollars per year. Although Midwestern communities are also increasingly impacted by larger events that can alone meet the billion-dollar-disaster threshold, the Midwest has not had the level of community resilience planning experienced elsewhere. F3 advances community resilience planning approaches for capacity-limited communities, explores integration of renewable energy by municipal governments, and defined individual resilience actions that could be directed through with assistance of community-based organizations. Community Resilience Planning Currently, the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) two-part playbook to guide communities on resilience planning and different initiatives including San Francisco Bay Area Planning and Urban Research Association’s Resilient City (SPUR), Resilient Washington State (RWS), and Oregon Resilience Plan (ORP) represent the state-of-the-art approaches on community resilience planning. However, “...(they) do not advise on how to make resilience performance measurement frameworks operational” (Miles 2021).
